intro: Look around your room. A ball rolls. A door swings shut. A cup holds juice. A coat keeps rain off. Every one of these has a science story. This unit tells two of them.
First, pushes and pulls. Nothing moves on its own. Something pushes it or pulls it. You will learn how to start things, stop things, and turn things.
Then, stuff. Everything is made of some material. Hard or soft. Bendy or stiff. Soaks up water or not. You will learn to describe stuff, sort it, and pick the right stuff for a job.
bigQuestion: How do pushes, pulls and the right materials help us do things?

timeline.t: You push the blanket off. You pull on your socks.
You pour milk. It takes the shape of the bowl. The spoon keeps its shape.
You push the heavy door. It swings open. A big push works better than a little one.
Rain rolls off your coat. It does not soak in. Good material!
You kick a ball. It rolls. It bumps another ball. That one moves too.
An ice cube melts in your cup. Now it is water.
You sort buttons. Hard ones here. Soft cloth there.
A heavy box of books will not lift. You push it. It slides.
You build a block tower. Then you take it apart. Same blocks.
An egg cooks in the pan. It turns white. It will not turn back.
You pull up the blanket. A pull brings it close.

words.d: to press on a thing and move it away from you
to tug on a thing and move it toward you
a push or a pull
the way a thing is going
something you can see or feel about a thing, like its color or how hard it is
to soak up water like a sponge
a thing that keeps its own shape, like a block
a thing that pours and takes the shape of its cup, like water

test.why: A force is a push or a pull. Forces make things move.

test.q: A pull moves a thing which way?
test.why: When you pull, you tug on a thing. It comes toward you.

test.q: You want a toy car to go far. What do you do?
test.why: A big push makes a big change. The car goes far.

test.q: A ball hits a wall and comes back. What did the wall do?
choices: It pushed the ball a new way
It pulled the ball into the wall
test.why: The wall pushed back on the ball. That push changed its direction.

test.q: Which is a property of a rock?
test.why: A rock is hard. It does not pour or soak up water.

test.q: Why is paper a bad raincoat?
test.why: Paper absorbs water. It gets soggy in the rain.

test.q: Which one keeps its own shape?
test.why: A block is a solid. Solids keep their own shape.

test.q: A box is too heavy to lift. What can help?
test.why: You can push the box up a ramp instead of lifting it.
Cool melted butter and it gets hard again. Eggs and toast stay changed.

test.q: A rolling ball bumps a still ball. What happens?
choices: The still ball starts to move
test.why: Things that touch can push each other. The rolling ball pushes the still one.

write.prompt: Pick the best material for a toy boat: paper, sponge or plastic. Say which one you pick. Tell what you saw happen in the water. Tell why that makes it the best.
tips: Claim: say which material you pick.
Evidence: tell what happened to each one in the water.
Reasoning: say what property makes your pick float.
The other side: say why one of the others would not work.

title: Pushes, Pulls and Stuff

chapters.title: Pushes and Pulls
chapters.bigQuestion: What makes things start, stop and change the way they go?

story.title: Who Is Pushing? Who Is Pulling?
story.kicker: Come to the playground. Look close. Someone is pushing. Someone is pulling.
paragraphs: It is recess at a school in Chicago. The playground is full. Ana sits on a swing. Her friend Leo stands behind her. Leo pushes the swing. Ana flies up. She comes back down. Leo pushes again.
Over by the fence, Sam has a wagon. It is full of balls. Sam grabs the handle. He pulls. The wagon rolls along. It bumps over a crack. Sam pulls harder. The wagon keeps going.
Near the slide, a soccer ball sits still. Mia runs up. She kicks it. The ball zooms across the grass. It hits the wall. It bounces back. Now it rolls the other way.
Look around. Every moving thing got a push or a pull. The swing. The wagon. The ball. Nothing started moving on its own. Somebody made it move.
story.think: Pick one thing on your playground. Who pushes it? Who pulls it?

lessons.title: A Push Makes It Go
lessons.mainIdea: A push moves a thing away from you.
reading: A ball sits on the floor. It does not move. It waits. Then you push it. Your hand moves it away from you. Now the ball rolls. Your push made it go.
A *push* is a *force*. A force is what makes things move. When you push, you press on a thing. You move it away from you. A push can be small. A push can be big.
Look for pushes. You push a door open. You push a cart. You push a button. You push off the wall in a pool. Pushes are everywhere.

words.d: to press on a thing and move it away from you
a push or a pull

look.title: The Shopping Cart
look.text: Look at the cart in the store. It is empty. It sits still. A girl puts her hands on the handle. She pushes. The cart rolls down the aisle. She pushes more. It goes faster.
look.prompt: What made the cart start to move?

check.q: What made the ball roll?
check.why: The ball sat still until a hand pushed it. The push made it go.

check.q: Which one is a push?
check.why: Pressing the door moves it away from you. That is a push. Dragging and tugging are pulls.

check.q: A push moves a thing which way?
check.why: When you push, you press on a thing. It moves away from you.

lessons.title: A Pull Makes It Come
lessons.mainIdea: A pull moves a thing toward you.
reading: A wagon sits on the grass. You grab the handle. You pull. The wagon comes toward you. It rolls along behind you. Your pull made it go.
A *pull* is a force too. When you pull, you tug on a thing. You move it toward you. You pull a rope. You pull a zipper. You pull a dog on a leash.
A push and a pull are both forces. A push sends a thing away. A pull brings a thing closer. Both can start a thing moving.

words.d: to tug on a thing and move it toward you

look.title: Tug of War
look.text: Two teams hold one long rope. Each team pulls. The rope moves a little this way. Then a little that way. Then the red team pulls harder. The rope slides toward the red team. The blue team slides too!
look.prompt: Why did the rope move toward the red team?

check.q: Which one is a pull?
check.why: Tugging the handle brings the wagon toward you. That is a pull.

check.q: A pull moves a thing which way?
check.why: When you pull, you tug on a thing. It comes toward you.

check.q: What do a push and a pull both do?
choices: They both send a thing away
They both bring a thing closer
They both can start a thing moving
check.why: A push and a pull are both forces. Both can make a still thing start to move.

lessons.title: Making It Stop
lessons.mainIdea: A push or a pull can stop a moving thing.
reading: A ball rolls toward you. You put out your hands. The ball hits your hands. Your hands push back. The ball stops. A push stopped it.
A moving thing keeps going. It needs a force to *stop*. A wall can push on a ball. The grass rubs on a ball. Your hands can catch a ball. Each one is a push that makes the ball stop.
Pulls can stop things too. A dog runs. The leash goes tight. The leash pulls the dog. The dog stops.

words.d: to end moving and hold still

look.title: The Rolling Ball
look.text: A ball rolls across the gym floor. It goes and goes. Then it rolls onto the thick mat. The mat rubs on it. The ball slows down. It stops. It never rolls far on the mat.
look.prompt: Why did the ball stop on the mat?

check.q: What stops a rolling ball?
choices: Only the color of the ball
check.why: A moving thing needs a force to stop. Hands, a wall or grass can push on it.

check.q: The leash goes tight. What happens to the running dog?
choices: The dog keeps running the same way
check.why: The tight leash pulls on the dog. The pull stops the dog.

check.q: You catch a ball. What do your hands do?
choices: Pull the ball to go faster
Push on the ball to stop it
check.why: Your hands push back on the ball. That push makes it stop.

lessons.title: Big Push, Little Push
lessons.mainIdea: A bigger push makes a bigger change.
reading: Tap a toy car. It rolls a little. It stops fast. Now push the car hard. It zooms across the room. It goes far. The big push made a big change.
A small push makes a small change. A big push makes a big change. The same is true for pulls. Pull a wagon gently. It creeps. Pull it hard. It jumps forward.
Try it. Roll a ball with a soft push. Mark where it stops. Roll it with a hard push. Mark again. Which mark is farther? That is your *evidence*.

words.d: what you see or measure that shows an idea is true

look.title: Two Kicks
look.text: Jae kicks a ball softly. It rolls to the cone. Then Jae kicks the same ball hard. It rolls past the cone. It rolls past the tree. It rolls all the way to the fence.
look.prompt: Which kick was bigger? How do you know?

check.q: You want the car to go far. What should you do?
check.why: A big push makes a big change. The hard push sends the car far.

check.q: A soft push makes what kind of change?
check.why: A small push makes a small change. The car moves only a little.

check.q: Jae's ball rolled to the fence. What does that show?
check.why: The ball went far. A big push makes a big change. So the kick was hard.

lessons.title: Changing Direction
lessons.mainIdea: A push or a pull can change which way a thing goes.
reading: A ball rolls to the left. You tap it with your foot. Now it rolls to the right. Your push changed its *direction*. Direction is the way a thing goes.
Kick a ball at a wall. The wall pushes back. The ball bounces off. It comes back a new way. A push can turn a moving thing.
Pulls turn things too. A kite flies straight. You pull the string. The kite swoops to the side. The pull changed its direction.

words.d: the way a thing is going

look.title: Ball on the Wall
look.text: Look at the ball. It rolls straight at the wall. Bump! It hits the wall. Now it rolls back toward you. The ball did not roll through the wall. The wall pushed it back.
look.prompt: What changed the direction of the ball?

check.q: What is direction?
choices: The way a thing is going
check.why: Direction is the way a thing goes, like left or right.

check.q: A ball hits a wall and bounces back. What did the wall do?
choices: It pushed the ball a new way
It made the ball stop for good
check.why: The wall pushed back on the ball. The push sent it a new direction.

check.q: You pull a kite string. What can happen?
check.why: A pull can turn a moving thing. The kite swoops to the side.

lessons.title: Ball Meets Ball
lessons.mainIdea: Things that touch can push each other.
reading: A blue ball sits still. A red ball rolls at it. Bump! The red ball pushes the blue ball. The blue ball starts to roll. The red ball slows down.
Balls that *touch* can push each other. Blocks can push each other too. So can toy cars. When two things bump, each one pushes the other.
You can plan a bump. Roll a marble at a block. The block moves. Aim well. You can knock down a tower with one marble.

words.d: to bump into or press on another thing

look.title: The Bowling Ball
look.text: Look at the pins. They stand in a row. A bowling ball rolls down the lane. It hits the first pin. That pin falls into the next pin. That pin falls too. Soon they are all down.
look.prompt: What pushed the last pin? It never touched the ball.

check.q: The red ball rolls into the blue ball. What happens?
choices: The blue ball starts to move
check.why: The red ball pushes the blue ball when they touch. The push makes it roll.

check.q: When two balls bump, which one pushes?
check.why: When two things bump, each one pushes the other. The red ball slows down too.

check.q: The bowling ball hits one pin. How do the other pins fall?
choices: Each pin pushes the next one
check.why: Each falling pin touches the next pin and pushes it over.

lessons.title: Ramps and Heavy Boxes
lessons.mainIdea: A push can solve a problem, like moving a heavy box.
reading: A big box sits on the floor. It is too heavy to lift. What can you do? Push it! Get low. Put your hands on the box. Push with your legs. The box slides.
Still too heavy? Ask a friend. Two pushes are bigger than one. Or put the box on a cart. Wheels roll. A cart makes pushing easy.
A *ramp* helps too. A ramp is a flat slope. Push the box up the ramp. It is easier than lifting. Movers use ramps every day.

words.d: a flat slope that goes from low to high

look.title: The Moving Truck
look.text: A moving truck is parked on a street in Chicago. A long ramp goes from the ground to the truck. Two movers push a couch up the ramp. It rolls on a cart with wheels. Up it goes. No one has to lift the couch.
look.prompt: Why do the movers use a ramp and wheels?

check.q: A box is too heavy to lift. What can you try?
check.why: You do not have to lift it. A push can slide the box across the floor.

check.q: Two friends push together. What kind of push is that?
check.why: Two pushes are bigger than one. A bigger push moves a heavier box.

check.q: What does a ramp help you do?
choices: Move a box up without lifting it
check.why: A ramp is a slope. You push the box up it instead of lifting it.

review.why: A force is a push or a pull. Forces make things move, stop and turn.

review.q: A push moves a thing which way?
review.why: A push presses on a thing and sends it away from you.

review.q: You want a ball to go far. What push do you use?
review.why: A big push makes a big change. The hard push sends the ball far.

review.q: A ball rolls onto thick grass and stops. Why?
choices: The grass pushed on the ball
review.why: The grass rubs on the ball. That push slows it down until it stops.

review.q: A rolling ball bumps a still ball. What happens to the still ball?
review.why: Things that touch can push each other. The rolling ball pushes the still one.

review.q: A box is too heavy to lift into a truck. What helps most?
review.why: A ramp lets you push the box up instead of lifting it.

chapters.title: What Things Are Made Of
chapters.bigQuestion: How do we pick the right stuff to build with?

story.title: The Cushion Fort
story.kicker: Rain is falling. Three kids build a fort in the living room. What will they use?
paragraphs: It is raining in Chicago. Rosa, Ben and Kim cannot go outside. So they build a fort. Rosa pulls the cushions off the couch. Ben brings a box of wooden blocks. Kim drags in a big soft blanket.
Ben stacks the blocks. They are hard. They stand up straight. He makes two towers. Rosa leans the cushions on the towers. The cushions are soft. They bend a little. They do not fall.
Kim throws the blanket over the top. The blanket is thin and floppy. It cannot stand up on its own. But it makes a great roof. The fort is dark inside. Perfect.
Later, they take it all apart. The cushions go back on the couch. The blocks go in the box. The blanket goes on the bed. Tomorrow they can build again.
story.think: Why did they use blocks for the walls and a blanket for the roof?

lessons.title: Hard, Soft, Rough, Smooth
lessons.mainIdea: You can describe a material by how it looks and feels.
reading: Pick up a rock. It is hard. Pick up a pillow. It is soft. Rub a brick. It is rough. Rub a spoon. It is smooth. These are *properties*. A property is a way to describe a thing.
A *material* is the stuff a thing is made of. Color is a property. Hard or soft is a property. Rough or smooth is a property. Your eyes and hands find the properties.
Try it. Close your eyes. A friend puts a thing in your hand. Feel it. Hard or soft? Rough or smooth? Can you guess what it is?

words.d: something you can see or feel about a thing, like its color or how hard it is
the stuff a thing is made of

look.title: Two Cups
look.text: Look at two cups. One is glass. It is hard and smooth. Tap it. It clinks. The other is paper. It is soft. You can bend it. Squeeze it and it folds. Both cups hold juice.
look.prompt: Name two ways the cups are different.

check.q: Which one of these is a property?
check.why: Rough or smooth is a way to describe a thing. A spoon and a pillow are things.

check.q: How do you find out if a thing is rough?
check.why: Your hands feel rough and smooth. Rub the thing to find out.

check.q: What is a material?
choices: The stuff a thing is made of
check.why: A material is the stuff a thing is made of, like wood or glass.

lessons.title: Does It Bend? Does It Soak?
lessons.mainIdea: Some materials bend and some soak up water.
reading: Bend a rubber band. It stretches. Let go. It snaps back. Bend a stick. It does not bend much. Push harder. Snap! It breaks. Rubber bends. Wood does not.
Drip water on a paper towel. The water sinks in. The towel gets wet. It *absorbs* the water. Drip water on a plastic plate. The water sits on top. It rolls off. Plastic does not absorb water.
Bendy or stiff is a property. Absorbs water or not is a property. You can test both. Bend it. Drip on it. Watch what happens.

words.d: to soak up water like a sponge

look.title: The Spill
look.text: Milk spills on the table. Dad grabs a paper towel. He presses it on the milk. The towel turns wet and heavy. The milk is gone from the table. Then he tries a plastic bag. The milk just slides around.
look.prompt: Why did the paper towel work and the plastic bag did not?

check.q: What does absorb mean?
check.why: Absorb means to soak up water, like a towel or a sponge.

check.q: Which one soaks up water?
check.why: Water sinks into a paper towel. It rolls off plastic and glass.

check.q: What happens when you bend a rubber band and let go?
check.why: Rubber bends and stretches. When you let go, it snaps back.

lessons.title: Sorting Things
lessons.mainIdea: We can sort things into groups by their properties.
reading: Dump out a box of stuff. Buttons, rocks, cotton balls, spoons. Now *sort* them. Put the hard things here. Put the soft things there. You made two groups.
You can sort by any property. Sort by color. Sort by rough or smooth. Sort by what bends. The same button can go in many groups. It is red. It is hard. It is smooth.
Sorting helps us see patterns. All the metal things are hard and shiny. All the cloth things are soft. A *pattern* is something that happens again and again.

words.d: to put things into groups that are alike
something that happens the same way again and again

look.title: The Sock Drawer
look.text: Look in the drawer. Socks are everywhere. Big socks. Little socks. Wool socks. Thin socks. Mom sorts them. All the big ones go left. All the little ones go right. Now she sorts the big ones by color.
look.prompt: What property did Mom use first? What did she use next?

check.q: What does it mean to sort?
choices: To put things in groups that are alike
check.why: Sorting means putting things that are alike into the same group.

check.q: A rock is gray, hard and rough. Which group can it go in?
check.why: The rock is hard. So it goes in the hard group.

check.q: Every metal spoon is hard and shiny. What is that called?
check.why: It happens the same way again and again. That is a pattern.

sections.title: The Right Stuff for the Job

lessons.title: A Raincoat and a Window
lessons.mainIdea: We pick a material because of its properties.
reading: It is raining. You need a coat. Would a paper coat work? No. Paper absorbs water. It gets soggy. A rubber coat works. Water rolls off. Rubber does not absorb water.
A window lets in light. You need to see through it. Wood is hard but you cannot see through it. Glass is hard and *clear*. Glass is the right material for a window.
Think about the job. Then think about the properties. A pillow needs soft. A hammer needs hard. A towel needs to absorb. Match the material to the job.

words.d: easy to see through, like glass

look.title: Choose a Boat
look.text: You want to make a toy boat. You have a paper cup, a sponge and a plastic tub. You put each one in water. The paper cup gets soggy and sinks. The sponge fills with water. The plastic tub floats all day.
look.prompt: Which one makes the best boat? Why?

check.q: Why is rubber good for a raincoat?
check.why: Rubber does not absorb water. Rain rolls off and you stay dry.

check.q: Why is glass good for a window?
check.why: You can see through glass. It is also hard, so it keeps out wind.

check.q: You need a towel. What property matters most?
check.why: A towel's job is to dry things. It must soak up water.

lessons.title: Solids and Liquids
lessons.mainIdea: A solid keeps its shape. A liquid takes the shape of its cup.
reading: A block is a *solid*. Put it in a cup. It is still a block. Put it in a bowl. Still a block. A solid keeps its own shape.
Water is a *liquid*. Pour it in a cup. It is cup-shaped. Pour it in a bowl. Now it is bowl-shaped. A liquid takes the shape of what holds it.
Liquids pour. Solids do not pour. Milk pours. Juice pours. A spoon does not pour. A rock does not pour. Watch it. That is the test.

words.d: a thing that keeps its own shape, like a block
a thing that pours and takes the shape of its cup, like water

look.title: Juice and Ice
look.text: Look at a tall glass of juice. Pour it into a wide bowl. The juice spreads out flat. Now drop an ice cube in the glass. Move the ice cube to the bowl. It is still a cube. Same shape.
look.prompt: Which one is a solid? Which one is a liquid? How do you know?

check.q: Which one is a solid?
check.why: A block keeps its own shape. Milk and juice pour.

check.q: You pour water into a bowl. What shape is the water?
check.why: A liquid takes the shape of what holds it. In a bowl it is bowl-shaped.

check.q: What is one way to tell a liquid?
check.why: Liquids pour. Solids do not.

lessons.title: Small Pieces, Big Things
lessons.mainIdea: A big thing can be built from small pieces and taken apart again.
reading: One block is small. Stack ten blocks. Now you have a tower. Stack more. Now it is a castle. Big things can be built from small *pieces*.
You can take a big thing apart too. Knock down the tower. Now you have ten blocks again. Build a bridge with them. Then a boat. The same pieces make many things.
A brick house is like this. Each brick is small. Thousands of bricks make a wall. Look at the bricks on a building in your town. Count a row.

words.d: one small part of a bigger thing

look.title: The Puzzle
look.text: Look at the puzzle box. Inside are 24 small pieces. Each one is a funny shape. Put them together. Now there is one big picture of a dog. Take it apart. It is 24 pieces again.
look.prompt: Can the same 24 pieces make the dog picture again? Why?

check.q: What can you build from many small blocks?
check.why: Small pieces stack up into a big thing, like a tower.

check.q: You knock down a block tower. What do you have?
check.why: Taking a thing apart gives you the same pieces back.

check.q: A brick wall is made of what?
check.why: Each brick is small. Many bricks together make a wall.

lessons.title: Heat It, Cool It
lessons.mainIdea: Heating and cooling change things. Some changes go back. Some do not.
reading: Put an ice cube in the sun. It *melts*. Now it is water. Put the water in the freezer. It gets cold. It turns back into ice. This change can go back.
Butter is like this too. Warm it. It melts. Cool it. It gets hard again. Ice and butter can go back and forth.
Now cook an egg. The clear part turns white. It gets firm. Cool the egg. It stays cooked. It will not turn runny again. Some changes do not go back. Burnt toast stays burnt.

words.d: to turn from a solid into a liquid when it gets warm

look.title: Hot and Cold
look.prompt: Which one is hottest? Which one is coldest?

check.q: You put ice in the sun. What happens?
check.why: The sun warms the ice. Warm ice melts into water.

check.q: Which change can go back?
check.why: Cool the melted butter and it gets hard again. Toast and eggs stay changed.

check.q: You cool a cooked egg. What happens?
check.why: Cooking an egg is a change that does not go back.

choices: A way to describe a thing, like hard or soft
review.why: A property is something you can see or feel about a thing.
Paper towels absorb water. Water rolls off plastic and glass.

review.q: Why is glass a good window?
review.why: Glass is clear. Light comes in and you can see out.

review.q: Which one takes the shape of its cup?
review.why: Milk is a liquid. A liquid takes the shape of what holds it.

review.q: You take apart a block castle. What can you do next?
choices: Build something new with the blocks
review.why: The same pieces can be built into many different things.

review.q: Which change does not go back?
review.why: Burnt toast stays burnt. Ice and butter can go back to solid.
